claim: Spiny projection neurons (SPNs) in dorsal striatum are often proposed as a locus of reinforcement learning in the basal ganglia.
source: Spiny projection neurons (SPNs) in dorsal striatum are often proposed as a locus of reinforcement learning in the basal ganglia.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature in the introduction section.

claim: Direct-pathway (dSPN) and indirect-pathway (iSPN) neurons promote and suppress actions, respectively.
source: Direct-pathway (dSPN) and indirect-pathway (iSPN) neurons, which promote and suppress actions, respectively, exhibit synaptic plasticity that reinforces activity associated with elevated or suppressed dopamine release.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to perturbation studies (Kravitz et al., 2010; Freeze et al., 2013; Lee and Sabatini, 2021) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: dSPN and iSPN neurons exhibit synaptic plasticity that reinforces activity associated with elevated or suppressed dopamine release.
source: Direct-pathway (dSPN) and indirect-pathway (iSPN) neurons, which promote and suppress actions, respectively, exhibit synaptic plasticity that reinforces activity associated with elevated or suppressed dopamine release.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies (Shen et al., 2008; Frank, 2005; Iino et al., 2020) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: iSPN plasticity prevents successful learning as it reinforces activity patterns associated with negative outcomes.
source: We show that iSPN plasticity prevents successful learning, as it reinforces activity patterns associated with negative outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical analysis and simulations presented in Figures 2 and related text.

claim: Pathological iSPN learning behavior is reversed if functionally opponent dSPNs and iSPNs are simultaneously activated by efferent input following action selection.
source: However, this pathological behavior is reversed if functionally opponent dSPNs and iSPNs, which promote and suppress the current behavior, are simultaneously activated by efferent input following action selection.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical analysis and simulations presented in Figure 3 and related text.

claim: The prediction that opponent dSPNs and iSPNs are co-active following action selection is supported by striatal recordings.
source: This prediction is supported by striatal recordings and contrasts with prior models of SPN representations.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of experimental data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The basal ganglia is a reinforcement learning system.
source: Numerous studies have proposed that the basal ganglia is a reinforcement learning system (Joel et al., 2002; Niv, 2009; Ito and Doya, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SPNs receive diverse contextual information from the cerebral cortex.
source: Spiny projection neurons (SPNs) in the striatum are well-positioned to take part in such an algorithm, as they receive diverse contextual information from the cerebral cortex and are involved in both action selection (in dorsal striatum; Packard and Knowlton, 2002; Seo et al., 2012; Balleine et al., 2007) and value prediction (in ventral striatum; Cardinal et al., 2002; Montague et al., 1996; O'Doherty et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SPNs are involved in action selection in dorsal striatum.
source: Spiny projection neurons (SPNs) in the striatum are well-positioned to take part in such an algorithm, as they receive diverse contextual information from the cerebral cortex and are involved in both action selection (in dorsal striatum; Packard and Knowlton, 2002; Seo et al., 2012; Balleine et al., 2007) and value prediction (in ventral striatum; Cardinal et al., 2002; Montague et al., 1996; O'Doherty et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SPNs are involved in value prediction in ventral striatum.
source: Spiny projection neurons (SPNs) in the striatum are well-positioned to take part in such an algorithm, as they receive diverse contextual information from the cerebral cortex and are involved in both action selection (in dorsal striatum; Packard and Knowlton, 2002; Seo et al., 2012; Balleine et al., 2007) and value prediction (in ventral striatum; Cardinal et al., 2002; Montague et al., 1996; O'Doherty et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Plasticity of SPN input synapses is modulated by midbrain dopamine release.
source: Moreover, plasticity of SPN input synapses is modulated by midbrain dopamine release (Wickens et al., 1996; Calabresi et al., 2000; Contreras-Vidal and Schultz, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental literature.

claim: Midbrain dopamine release reflects reward prediction error.
source: A variety of studies support the view that this dopamine release reflects reward prediction error (Schultz et al., 1997; Montague et al., 1996; Houk and Adams, 1995), which in many reinforcement learning algorithms is the key quantity used to modulate learning (Sutton and Barto, 2018; Niv, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: dSPNs and iSPNs exert opponent effects on action based on perturbation data.
source: These two classes of SPNs exert opponent effects on action based on perturbation data (Kravitz et al., 2010; Freeze et al., 2013; Lee and Sabatini, 2021), but also exhibit highly correlated activity (Cui et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental literature.

claim: dSPNs and iSPNs exhibit highly correlated activity.
source: These two classes of SPNs exert opponent effects on action based on perturbation data (Kravitz et al., 2010; Freeze et al., 2013; Lee and Sabatini, 2021), but also exhibit highly correlated activity (Cui et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental literature.

claim: dSPNs and iSPNs express different dopamine receptors (D1- and D2-type).
source: Moreover, dSPNs and iSPNs express different dopamine receptors (D1- and D2-type) and thus undergo synaptic plasticity according to different rules.
evidence: This is established knowledge about striatal neuron types.

claim: dSPN inputs are potentiated when coincident pre- and post-synaptic activity is followed by above-baseline dopamine activity.
source: In particular, dSPN inputs are potentiated when coincident pre- and post-synaptic activity is followed by above-baseline dopamine activity, while iSPN inputs are potentiated when coincident pre- and post-synaptic activity is followed by dopamine suppression (Shen et al., 2008; Frank, 2005; Iino et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental literature.

claim: iSPN inputs are potentiated when coincident pre- and post-synaptic activity is followed by dopamine suppression.
source: In particular, dSPN inputs are potentiated when coincident pre- and post-synaptic activity is followed by above-baseline dopamine activity, while iSPN inputs are potentiated when coincident pre- and post-synaptic activity is followed by dopamine suppression (Shen et al., 2008; Frank, 2005; Iino et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental literature.

claim: Prior studies have proposed that dSPNs learn from positive reinforcement to promote actions, and iSPNs learn from negative reinforcement to suppress actions.
source: Prior studies have proposed that dSPNs learn from positive reinforcement to promote actions, and iSPNs learn from negative reinforcement to suppress actions (Cruz et al., 2022; Collins and Frank, 2014; Jaskir and Frank, 2023; Varin et al., 2023; Mikhael and Bogacz, 2016; Dunovan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A straightforward implementation of the model where dSPNs learn from positive reinforcement and iSPNs learn from negative reinforcement fails to yield a functional reinforcement learning algorithm.
source: However, we will show that a straightforward implementation of such a model fails to yield a functional reinforcement learning algorithm, as the iSPN learning rule assigns blame for negative outcomes to the wrong actions.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical analysis and simulations presented in Figure 2.

claim: The iSPN learning rule assigns blame for negative outcomes to the wrong actions.
source: However, we will show that a straightforward implementation of such a model fails to yield a functional reinforcement learning algorithm, as the iSPN learning rule assigns blame for negative outcomes to the wrong actions.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical analysis and simulations presented in Figure 2.

claim: The model provides an explanation for the apparent paradox that the activities of dSPNs and iSPNs are positively correlated despite their opponent causal functions.
source: This decomposition provides an explanation for the apparent paradox that the activities of dSPNs and iSPNs are positively correlated despite their opponent causal functions (Cui et al., 2013), and provides a solution to the problem of multiplexing signals related to behavioral execution and learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by the theoretical model and analysis of experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The model predicts that dSPNs and iSPNs that are responsible for regulating the same behavior should be co-active following action selection.
source: The model also makes predictions about the time course of SPN activity, including that dSPNs and iSPNs that are responsible for regulating the same behavior (promoting and suppressing it, respectively) should be co-active following action selection.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the theoretical model.

claim: The prediction that dSPNs and iSPNs responsible for regulating the same behavior are co-active contrasts with prior proposals that dSPNs that promote an action are co-active with iSPNs that suppress different actions.
source: This somewhat counterintuitive prediction contrasts with prior proposals that dSPNs that promote an action are co-active with iSPNs that suppress different actions (Mink, 1996; Redgrave et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and comparison with the current model.

claim: Support for the prediction of co-active opponent dSPNs and iSPNs is found in experimental recordings of dSPNs and iSPNs during spontaneous behavior.
source: We find support for this prediction in experimental recordings of dSPNs and iSPNs during spontaneous behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of experimental data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The nonuniformity of dSPN and iSPN plasticity rules enables more sophisticated learning algorithms than can be achieved in models with a single plasticity rule.
source: Next, we show that the nonuniformity of dSPN and iSPN plasticity rules enables more sophisticated learning algorithms than can be achieved in models with a single plasticity rule.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical analysis and simulations presented in Figure 7.

claim: The nonuniformity of dSPN and iSPN plasticity rules enables the striatum to implement off-policy reinforcement learning algorithms.
source: In particular, it enables the striatum to implement so-called off-policy reinforcement learning algorithms, in which the corticostriatal pathway learns from the the outcomes of actions that are driven by other neural pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical analysis and simulations presented in Figure 7.

claim: Off-policy algorithms are commonly used in state-of-the-art machine learning models as they dramatically improve learning efficiency.
source: Off-policy algorithms are commonly used in state-of-the-art machine learning models, as they dramatically improve learning efficiency by facilitating learning from expert demonstrations, mixture-of-experts models, and replayed experiences (Arulkumaran et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Off-policy algorithms require a dopaminergic signal in dorsal striatum that combines classic state-based reward prediction error with a form of action prediction error.
source: Following the implications of this model further, we show that off-policy algorithms require a dopaminergic signal in dorsal striatum that combines classic state-based reward prediction error with a form of action prediction error.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical analysis and simulations presented in Figure 7.

claim: A key signature of the prediction that dopamine combines state-based and action prediction error is confirmed in recent dopamine data collected from dorsolateral striatum during spontaneous behavior.
source: We confirm a key signature of this prediction in recent dopamine data collected from dorsolateral striatum (DLS) during spontaneous behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 7E.

claim: Plasticity of corticostriatal synapses is modeled using a three-factor learning rule dependent on coincident presynaptic activity, post-synaptic activity, and dopamine release.
source: In line with previous experimental (Wickens et al., 1996; Calabresi et al., 2000; Contreras-Vidal and Schultz, 1999) and modeling (Sutton and Barto, 2018; Niv, 2009) studies, we model plasticity of corticostriatal synapses using a three-factor learning rule, dependent on coincident presynaptic activity, post-synaptic activity, and dopamine release (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental and modeling literature.

claim: For dSPNs, the propensity of input synapses to potentiate increases with increasing dopamine concentration.
source: For dSPNs, the propensity of input synapses to potentiate increases with increasing dopamine concentration, while for iSPNs the opposite is true.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental literature.

claim: For iSPNs, the propensity of input synapses to potentiate decreases with increasing dopamine concentration.
source: For dSPNs, the propensity of input synapses to potentiate increases with increasing dopamine concentration, while for iSPNs the opposite is true.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental literature.

claim: The observation that dSPN and iSPN plasticity have opposite dependence on dopamine is corroborated by converging evidence from observations of dendritic spine volume, intracellular PKA measurements, and spike-timing-dependent plasticity protocols.
source: This observation is corroborated by converging evidence from observations of dendritic spine volume, intracellular PKA measurements, and spike-timing-dependent plasticity protocols (Shen et al., 2008; Gurney et al., 2015; Iino et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental literature.

claim: Prior work has proposed that dSPNs activate when actions are performed and iSPNs activate when actions are suppressed.
source: Prior work has proposed that dSPNs activate when actions are performed and iSPNs activate when actions are suppressed (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: When an animal selects among multiple actions, subpopulations of dSPNs are thought to promote the selected action, while other subpopulations of iSPNs inhibit the unchosen actions.
source: When an animal selects among multiple actions, subpopulations of dSPNs are thought to promote the selected action, while other subpopulations of iSPNs inhibit the unchosen actions (Mink, 1996; Redgrave et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The canonical action selection model, when combined with the three-factor plasticity rules, fails to produce a functional reinforcement learning algorithm.
source: We refer to this general description as the 'canonical action selection model' of SPN activity and show that this model, when combined with the plasticity rules above, fails to produce a functional reinforcement learning algorithm.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical analysis and simulations presented in Figure 2.

claim: The failure of the canonical action selection model is specifically due to the iSPN plasticity rule.
source: This failure is specifically due to the iSPN plasticity rule.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical analysis and simulations presented in Figure 2.

claim: The SPN representation predicted by the canonical action selection model is inconsistent with recordings of identified dSPNs and iSPNs.
source: Later, we also show that the SPN representation predicted by the canonical action selection model is inconsistent with recordings of identified dSPNs and iSPNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of experimental data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The dSPN plasticity rule is consistent with successful reinforcement learning.
source: It is easy to see that the dSPN plasticity rule in Equation 1 is consistent with successful reinforcement learning (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical analysis and simulations presented in Figure 2A.

claim: The iSPN plasticity rule does not promote successful learning.
source: However, a more careful examination reveals that the iSPN plasticity rule in Equation 2 does not promote successful learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical analysis and simulations presented in Figure 2B.

claim: In the canonical action selection model, dSPNs promoting a selected action and iSPNs inhibiting unselected actions are active.
source: In the canonical action selection model, dSPNs promoting a selected action and iSPNs inhibiting unselected actions are active.
evidence: This is a description of the canonical action selection model.

claim: If a negative outcome is encountered leading to a dopamine decrease, the iSPN plasticity rule predicts that inputs to iSPNs corresponding to unselected actions are strengthened.
source: If a negative outcome is encountered leading to a dopamine decrease, Equation 2 predicts that inputs to iSPNs corresponding to unselected actions are strengthened (LTP in Figure 2B, center).
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical analysis and illustration in Figure 2B.

claim: Strengthening iSPN inputs to unselected actions makes the action that led to the negative outcome more rather than less likely to be taken when the same cortical inputs are active in the future.
source: This makes the action that led to the negative outcome more rather than less likely to be taken when the same cortical inputs are active in the future (Figure 2B, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical analysis and illustration in Figure 2B.

claim: The plasticity rule of Equation 1 correctly reinforces dSPN activity patterns that lead to positive outcomes.
source: More generally, the model demonstrates that, while the plasticity rule of Equation 1 correctly reinforces dSPN activity patterns that lead to positive outcomes, Equation 2 incorrectly reinforces iSPN activity patterns that lead to negative outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical analysis and simulations.

claim: Equation 2 incorrectly reinforces iSPN activity patterns that lead to negative outcomes.
source: More generally, the model demonstrates that, while the plasticity rule of Equation 1 correctly reinforces dSPN activity patterns that lead to positive outcomes, Equation 2 incorrectly reinforces iSPN activity patterns that lead to negative outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical analysis and simulations.

claim: The function of iSPNs in inhibiting action does not change the fact that reinforcement of iSPN activity patterns leading to negative outcomes is undesirable.
source: The function of iSPNs in inhibiting action does not change the fact that such reinforcement is undesirable.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the analysis of iSPN plasticity.

claim: Depending on the learning rule, inputs to dSPNs that promote the selected action may be weakened following negative outcomes, which correctly disincentivizes the action that led to a negative outcome.
source: We note that, depending on the learning rule (Figure 1C), inputs to dSPNs that promote the selected action may be weakened (LTD in Figure 2B, left), which correctly disincentivizes the action that led to a negative outcome.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical analysis and illustration in Figure 2B.

claim: The dSPN effect of weakening inputs following negative outcomes competes with the pathological behavior of the iSPNs and is often unable to overcome it.
source: However, this dSPN effect competes with the pathological behavior of the iSPNs and is often unable to overcome it.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical analysis and simulations.

claim: If dopamine increases lead to depression of iSPN inputs, positive outcomes will lead to actions that were correctly being inhibited by iSPNs to be less inhibited in the future.
source: We also note that, if dopamine increases lead to depression of iSPN inputs (Figure 1A, center, right), positive outcomes will lead to actions that were correctly being inhibited by iSPNs to be less inhibited in the future.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the plasticity rules.

claim: Both positive and negative outcomes may cause incorrect iSPN learning.
source: Thus, both positive and negative outcomes may cause incorrect iSPN learning.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the analysis of iSPN plasticity.

claim: In the rectified model of dopamine dependence, pathological iSPN plasticity behavior still manifests when dopamine activity is suppressed.
source: In this case, pathological iSPN plasticity behavior still manifests when dopamine activity is suppressed (as in the examples of Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the rectified plasticity model.

claim: Dopamine activity was modeled as reward prediction error obtained using a temporal difference (TD) learning rule in simulations of learning tasks.
source: We simulated learning of multiple tasks with the three-factor plasticity rules above, with dopamine activity modeled as reward prediction error obtained using a temporal difference (TD) learning rule.
evidence: This describes the simulation methodology.

claim: In a go/no-go task with one cue in which the 'go' action is rewarded, the system learns the wrong behavior when negative performance feedback is provided on no-go trials.
source: In a go/no-go task with one cue in which the 'go' action is rewarded (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), the system learns the wrong behavior when negative performance feedback is provided on no-go trials, and thus iSPN plasticity is the main driver of learning (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented in Figure 2C.

claim: In a two-alternative forced choice task with rewards for correct actions, the system learns the task as dSPNs primarily drive the learning.
source: We also simulated a two-alternative forced choice task in which there are two cues (corresponding to different cortical input patterns), each with a corresponding target action. When performance feedback consists of rewards for correct actions, the system learns the task, as dSPNs primarily drive the learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented in Figure 2D.

claim: In a two-alternative forced choice task with punishments for incorrect actions, the system does not learn the task as iSPNs primarily drive the learning.
source: However, when instead performance feedback consists of giving punishments for incorrect actions, the system does not learn the task, as iSPNs primarily drive the learning (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented in Figure 2D.

claim: The problem of incorrect iSPN learning could in principle be avoided if the learning rate of iSPNs were very small compared to that of dSPNs.
source: We note that, in principle, this problem could be avoided if the learning rate of iSPNs were very small compared to that of dSPNs, ensuring that reinforcement learning is always primarily driven by the dSPN pathway (leaving iSPNs to potentially perform a different function).
evidence: This is a logical inference about an alternative solution.

claim: Having a very small iSPN learning rate would be inconsistent with prior studies indicating a significant role for the indirect pathway in reinforcement learning.
source: However, this alternative would be inconsistent with prior studies indicating a significant role for the indirect pathway in reinforcement learning (Peak et al., 2020; Lee and Sabatini, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The activity pattern that leads to correct learning about an action's outcome is different from the activity pattern that selects the action.
source: This implies that the activity pattern that leads to correct learning about an action's outcome is different from the activity pattern that selects the action.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the analysis of sum and difference modes.

claim: To promote or inhibit an action that leads to a dopamine increase or decrease, both dSPNs that promote and iSPNs that inhibit the action should be co-active.
source: To promote or inhibit, respectively, an action that leads to a dopamine increase or decrease, this analysis predicts that both dSPNs that promote and iSPNs that inhibit the action should be co-active.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the theoretical analysis.

claim: The key insight is that the pattern of SPN activity needed for learning involves simultaneous excitation of dSPNs that promote the current behavior and iSPNs that inhibit it.
source: The key insight of the above argument is that the pattern of SPN activity needed for learning involves simultaneous excitation of dSPNs that promote the current behavior and iSPNs that inhibit it.
evidence: This is a summary of the theoretical insight.

claim: The pattern of SPN activity needed for learning differs from the pattern of activity needed to drive selection of that behavior in the first place.
source: This differs from the pattern of activity needed to drive selection of that behavior in the first place.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the analysis.

claim: The model proposes that SPN activity contains a substantial efferent component that follows action selection and promotes learning, but has no causal impact on behavior.
source: We therefore propose a model in which SPN activity contains a substantial efferent component that follows action selection and promotes learning, but has no causal impact on behavior.
evidence: This is a key proposal of the model.

claim: In the model, feedforward corticostriatal inputs initially produce SPN activity whose difference mode causally influences action selection.
source: In the model, feedforward corticostriatal inputs initially produce SPN activity whose difference mode causally influences action selection, consistent with the canonical model (Figure 3A, left).
evidence: This describes a feature of the model illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: When an action is performed, both dSPNs and iSPNs responsible for promoting or inhibiting that action receive efferent excitatory input, producing sum mode activity.
source: When an action is performed, both dSPNs and iSPNs responsible for promoting or inhibiting that action receive efferent excitatory input, producing sum mode activity.
evidence: This describes a feature of the model.

claim: Following efferent input, SPN activity reflects both feedforward and efferent contributions.
source: Following this step, SPN activity reflects both contributions (Figure 3A, center).
evidence: This describes a feature of the model illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: The presence of sum mode activity leads to correct synaptic plasticity and learning.
source: The presence of sum mode activity leads to correct synaptic plasticity and learning (Figure 3A, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by the model and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: The efference model predicts an SPN representation in which, after an action is selected, the most highly active neurons are those responsible for regulating that behavior and not other behaviors.
source: Unlike the canonical action selection model (Figure 1A), this model thus predicts an SPN representation in which, after an action is selected, the most highly active neurons are those responsible for regulating that behavior and not other behaviors.
evidence: This is a prediction of the efference model.

claim: In SPN activity space, the sum and difference modes are orthogonal to one another.
source: In SPN activity space, the sum and difference modes are orthogonal to one another.
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the model.

claim: The orthogonality of sum and difference modes implies that encoding the action in the difference mode produces synaptic weight changes that do not promote learning.
source: This orthogonality has two consequences. First, it implies that encoding the action in the difference mode (as in the canonical action selection model) produces synaptic weight changes that do not promote learning, consistent with the competing effects of dSPN and iSPN plasticity that we previously described.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the orthogonality property.

claim: The orthogonality of sum and difference modes implies that adding efferent activity along the sum mode has no effect on action selection.
source: Second, it implies that adding efferent activity along the sum mode, which produces correct learning, has no effect on action selection.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the orthogonality property.

claim: The model provides a solution to the problem of interference between 'forward pass' (action selection) and 'backward pass' (learning) activity.
source: The model thus provides a solution to the problem of interference between 'forward pass' (action selection) and 'backward pass' (learning) activity, a common issue in models of biologically plausible learning algorithms (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a claim about the model's contribution to solving a known problem.

claim: The efference model solves go/no-go tasks regardless of the reward protocol.
source: In simulations, we confirm that unlike the canonical action selection model, this efference model solves go/no-go (Figure 3C) and action selection (Figure 3D) tasks regardless of the reward protocol.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented in Figure 3C.

claim: The efference model solves action selection tasks regardless of the reward protocol.
source: In simulations, we confirm that unlike the canonical action selection model, this efference model solves go/no-go (Figure 3C) and action selection (Figure 3D) tasks regardless of the reward protocol.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented in Figure 3D.

claim: The model enables successful learning even using a nonlinear model of SPN responses and a variety of plasticity rules.
source: Although the derivation above assumes linear SPN responses and linear dependences of plasticity on dopamine concentration, our model enables successful learning even using a nonlinear model of SPN responses and a variety of plasticity rules (Figure 3C, D; see Appendix for a derivation that explains this general success).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results and mathematical derivation.

claim: The results apply to cases in which actions are associated with distributed modes of dSPN and iSPN activity, and with a larger action space.
source: Finally, we also confirmed that our results apply to cases in which actions are associated with distributed modes of dSPN and iSPN activity, and with a larger action space (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The success of the model with distributed representations arises from the ability to form orthogonal subspaces for action selection and learning.
source: This success arises from the ability to form orthogonal subspaces for action selection and learning in this distributed setting.
evidence: This is an explanation for the model's success with distributed representations.

claim: Distributed representations are expected to be more faithful to neural recordings than discrete action spaces.
source: Although we describe the qualitative behavior of our model using discrete action spaces for illustrative purposes, we expect distributed representations to be more faithful to neural recordings.
evidence: This is a speculation about the biological relevance of distributed representations.

claim: A firing rate model of SPN activity was simulated in a two-alternative forced choice task.
source: We simulated a two-alternative forced choice task using a firing rate model of SPN activity.
evidence: This describes the simulation methodology.

claim: The selected action is determined by the difference mode activity of action-encoding SPNs during the first half of the stimulus presentation period.
source: The selected action is determined by the difference mode activity of action-encoding SPNs during the first half of the stimulus presentation period.
evidence: This describes a feature of the simulation.

claim: The sum mode is activated by efferent input during the second half of the stimulus presentation period.
source: The sum mode is activated by efferent input during the second half of this period.
evidence: This describes a feature of the simulation.

claim: The model learned the correct policy in about 10 trials.
source: The model learned the correct policy in about 10 trials.
evidence: This is a result from the simulation.

claim: Early in learning, difference mode activity is small and primarily driven by noise, leading to random action selection.
source: Early in learning, difference mode activity is small and primarily driven by noise, leading to random action selection (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: Sum mode activity is strongly driven after an action is selected, even early in learning.
source: However, sum mode activity is strongly driven after an action is selected (Figure 4B, bottom).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: As learning progresses, the magnitude of the difference mode activity evoked by the stimulus increases.
source: As learning progresses, the magnitude of the difference mode activity evoked by the stimulus increases (Figure 4B, third row).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: Late in learning, dSPN and iSPN firing rates are more separable during stimulus presentation, leading to correct action selection.
source: Late in learning, dSPN and iSPN firing rates are more separable during stimulus presentation, leading to correct action selection (Figure 4C, second row).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation illustrated in Figure 4C.

claim: Both difference and sum mode activity is evident late in learning, with the former leading the latter.
source: Both difference and sum mode activity is evident late in learning, with the former leading the latter (Figure 4C, bottom two rows).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation illustrated in Figure 4C.

claim: Throughout the learning process, difference and sum mode activity for the two actions are separable and non-interfering.
source: Throughout the learning process, difference and sum mode activity for the two actions are separable and non-interfering, even when both are present simultaneously.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation.

claim: Action selection is not disrupted by efferent feedback.
source: As a result, action selection is not disrupted by efferent feedback.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: The efference model multiplexes action selection and learning signals without separate learning phases or gated plasticity rules.
source: We conclude that the efference model multiplexes action selection and learning signals without separate learning phases or gated plasticity rules.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: The non-interference property enables learning based on delayed reward and efferent feedback from past actions even as the selection of subsequent actions unfolds.
source: While we illustrated this in a task with sequential trials for visualization purposes, this non-interference enables learning based on delayed reward and efferent feedback from past actions even as the selection of subsequent actions unfolds.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the model's capabilities.

claim: Simultaneous efferent input to opponent dSPNs and iSPNs is necessary for reinforcement learning, given known plasticity rules.
source: Thus far, we have provided theoretical arguments and model simulations that suggest that simultaneous efferent input to opponent dSPNs and iSPNs is necessary for reinforcement learning, given known plasticity rules.
evidence: This is a summary of the theoretical and simulation results.

claim: The dynamics predicted by the efference model are particularly important in scenarios where the action space is large and actions are selected continuously, without a clear trial structure.
source: We predict these dynamics to be particularly important in scenarios where the action space is large and actions are selected continuously, without a clear trial structure.
evidence: This is a prediction about when the model is most relevant.

claim: Data from a recent study recorded bulk and cellular dSPN and iSPN activity in spontaneously behaving mice.
source: We therefore used data from a recent study which recorded bulk and cellular dSPN and iSPN activity in spontaneously behaving mice (Figure 5A; Markowitz et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the experimental data used for analysis.

claim: No explicit rewards or task structure were provided during recording sessions in the spontaneous behavior study.
source: As no explicit rewards or task structure were provided during recording sessions, we adopted a modeling approach that makes minimal assumptions about the inputs to SPNs besides the core prediction of efferent activity.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: A network model was used in which populations of dSPNs and iSPNs promote or suppress different actions.
source: Specifically, we used a network model in which (1) populations of dSPNs and iSPNs promote or suppress different actions, (2) the feedforward inputs to all SPNs are random, (3) actions are sampled with log-likelihoods scaled according to the associated dSPN and iSPN difference mode, and (4) efferent activity excites the sum mode corresponding to the chosen action.
evidence: This describes the model used for analysis.

claim: In the model with random feedforward inputs, dSPN activity tends to lead to increased future iSPN activity.
source: In this model, difference mode dSPN and iSPN activity drives behaviors, and those behaviors cause efferent activation of the corresponding sum mode. As a result, on average, dSPN activity tends to lead to increased future iSPN activity, while iSPN activity leads to decreased future dSPN activity.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: In the model with random feedforward inputs, iSPN activity leads to decreased future dSPN activity.
source: In this model, difference mode dSPN and iSPN activity drives behaviors, and those behaviors cause efferent activation of the corresponding sum mode. As a result, on average, dSPN activity tends to lead to increased future iSPN activity, while iSPN activity leads to decreased future dSPN activity.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: The temporal cross-correlation between total dSPN and iSPN activity is asymmetric, with present dSPN activity correlating more strongly with future iSPN activity than with past iSPN activity.
source: Consequently, the temporal cross-correlation between total dSPN and iSPN activity is asymmetric, with present dSPN activity correlating more strongly with future iSPN activity than with past iSPN activity (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model illustrated in Figure 5B.

claim: Asymmetry in the temporal cross-correlation between dSPN and iSPN activity is not predicted by the canonical action selection model.
source: Such asymmetry is not predicted by the canonical action selection model, or models that assume dSPNs and iSPNs are co-active.
evidence: This is a comparison with alternative models.

claim: A skewed temporal cross-correlation similar to the model prediction is found in bulk two-color photometry recordings of dSPN and iSPN activity.
source: Computing the temporal cross-correlation in the bulk two-color photometry recordings of dSPN and iSPN activity, we find a very similar skewed relationship in the data (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: The skewed cross-correlation result is not an artifact of using different indicators for dSPN and iSPN activity.
source: We confirmed this result is not an artifact of the use of different indicators for dSPN and iSPN activity by repeating the analysis on data from mice where the indicators were reversed and finding the same result (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by control analysis presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The model predicts that both dSPNs and iSPNs exhibit similar selectivities in their tuning to actions.
source: Our model makes even stronger predictions about SPN population activity and its relationship to action selection. First, it predicts that both dSPNs and iSPNS exhibit similar selectivities in their tuning to actions.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model.

claim: The prediction of similar selectivities contrasts with implementations of the canonical action selection model in which iSPNs are more broadly tuned than dSPNs.
source: This contrasts with implementations of the canonical action selection model in which iSPNs are active whenever their associated action is not being performed and thus are more broadly tuned than dSPNs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a comparison with the canonical model.

claim: The model predicts that efferent activity excites dSPNs that promote the currently performed action and iSPNs that suppress the currently performed action.
source: Second, it also predicts that efferent activity excites dSPNs that promote the currently performed action and iSPNs that suppress the currently performed action.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model.

claim: dSPNs whose activity increases during a given action should tend to be above baseline shortly prior to the performance of that action.
source: As a result, dSPNs whose activity increases during the performance of a given action should tend to be above baseline shortly prior to the performance of that action.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: iSPNs whose activity increases during an action should tend to be below baseline during the time interval prior to action selection.
source: By contrast, iSPNs whose activity increases during an action should tend to be below baseline during the same time interval (Figure 6A, left; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a prediction of the model illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: The dSPNs and iSPNs whose activity increases during a given action should display negligible average fluctuations around the onset of other actions.
source: Moreover, this effect should be action-specific: the dSPNs and iSPNs whose activity increases during a given action should display negligible average fluctuations around the onset of other actions (Figure 6A, right).
evidence: This is a prediction of the model illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: The difference mode activity associated with an action is elevated prior to selection of that action.
source: These predictions can also be reinterpreted in terms of the sum and difference modes. The difference mode activity associated with an action is elevated prior to selection of that action, while the sum mode activity is excited following action selection (Figures 4C and 6B).
evidence: This is a prediction of the model illustrated in Figures 4C and 6B.

claim: The sum mode activity is excited following action selection.
source: These predictions can also be reinterpreted in terms of the sum and difference modes. The difference mode activity associated with an action is elevated prior to selection of that action, while the sum mode activity is excited following action selection (Figures 4C and 6B).
evidence: This is a prediction of the model illustrated in Figures 4C and 6B.

claim: The two phases of difference and sum mode activity are not predicted by the canonical action selection model.
source: These two phases of difference and sum mode activity are not predicted by the canonical action selection model.
evidence: This is a comparison with the canonical model.

claim: Calcium imaging data was collected during spontaneous mouse behavior and behavior was segmented into stereotyped kinematic motifs referred to as 'behavioral syllables'.
source: To test these hypotheses, we used calcium imaging data collected during spontaneous mouse behavior (Markowitz et al., 2018). The behavior of the mice was segmented into consistent, stereotyped kinematic motifs referred to as 'behavioral syllables', as in previous studies (Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes the experimental data used for analysis.

claim: Behavioral syllables are regarded as the analogs of actions in the model.
source: We regard these behavioral syllables as the analogs of actions in our model.
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Both dSPNs and iSPNs exhibit similar selectivities to different actions.
source: First, we examined the tuning of dSPNs and iSPNs to different actions and found that, broadly consistent with what our model predicts, both subpopulations exhibit similar selectivities (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: dSPN and iSPN population activity modes that increase during performance of a syllable were identified for each syllable.
source: Next, to test our predictions about dynamics before and after action selection (Figure 6A, B), we identified, for each syllable, dSPN and iSPN population activity vectors (modes) that increased the most during performance of that syllable (Figure 6C).
evidence: This describes the analysis method.

claim: The identified syllable-associated modes are meaningful as modes identified using two disjoint subsets of the data are correlated.
source: We confirmed that these modes are meaningful by checking that modes identified using two disjoint subsets of the data are correlated (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-validation analysis presented in Figure 6D.

claim: The activity of syllable-associated modes around the time of syllable onset displays remarkable agreement with the model prediction.
source: We then plotted the activity of these modes around the time of onset of the corresponding syllable, and averaged the result across the choice of syllables (Figure 6E). The result displays remarkable agreement with the model prediction in Figure 6A.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 6E.

claim: In a subset of mice where dSPNs and iSPNs were simultaneously recorded, the same qualitative results were found.
source: The majority of the above data consisted of recordings of either dSPNs or iSPNs from a given mouse. However, in a small subset (n = 4) of mice, dSPNs and iSPNs were simultaneously recorded and identified. We repeated the analysis above on these sessions, and found the same qualitative results (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 6F.

claim: The sum and difference mode activity visualized from simultaneous recordings agrees with the predictions of the model.
source: The simultaneous recordings further allowed us to visualize the sum and difference mode activity (Figure 6G), which also agrees with the predictions of our model (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 6G.

claim: Prior studies have argued for the importance of motor efference copies during basal ganglia learning, particularly when action selection is influenced by other brain regions.
source: Prior studies have argued for the importance of motor efference copies during basal ganglia learning, in particular when action selection is influenced by other brain regions (Fee, 2014; Lindsey and Litwin-Kumar, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Areas such as the motor cortex and cerebellum drive behavior independent of the basal ganglia.
source: Indeed, areas such as the motor cortex and cerebellum drive behavior independent of the basal ganglia (Exner et al., 2002; Wildgruber et al., 2001; Ashby et al., 2010; Silveri, 2021; Bostan and Strick, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Actions taken by an animal may at times differ from those most likely to be selected by striatal outputs.
source: Actions taken by an animal may therefore at times differ from those most likely to be selected by striatal outputs (Figure 7A), and it may be desirable for corticostriatal synapses to learn about the consequences of these actions.
evidence: This is a logical inference about behavior when multiple brain regions control actions.

claim: It may be desirable for corticostriatal synapses to learn about the consequences of actions that differ from those most likely to be selected by striatal outputs.
source: Actions taken by an animal may therefore at times differ from those most likely to be selected by striatal outputs (Figure 7A), and it may be desirable for corticostriatal synapses to learn about the consequences of these actions.
evidence: This is a speculation about desirable learning properties.

claim: Off-policy learning is learning in which the reinforcement learning system learns from actions that follow a different policy than its own.
source: In the reinforcement learning literature, this kind of learning is known as an 'off-policy' algorithm, as the reinforcement learning system (in our model, the striatum) learns from actions that follow a different policy than its own.
evidence: This is a definition from the reinforcement learning literature.

claim: Off-policy learning has been observed experimentally in the consolidation of cortically driven behaviors into subcortical circuits including DLS.
source: Off-policy learning has been observed experimentally, for instance in the consolidation of cortically driven behaviors into subcortical circuits including DLS (Kawai et al., 2015; Hwang et al., 2019; Mizes et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental literature.

claim: Off-policy learning requires efferent activity in SPNs that reflects the actions being performed, rather than the action that would be performed based on the striatum's influence alone.
source: Such learning requires efferent activity in SPNs that reflects the actions being performed, rather than the action that would be performed based on the striatum's influence alone.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for off-policy learning.

claim: Action selection was modeled as driven by weighted contributions from both the striatum and other motor pathways, with the ultimately selected action driving efferent activity.
source: We modeled this scenario by assuming that action selection is driven by weighted contributions from both the striatum and other motor pathways and that the ultimately selected action drives efferent activity (Figure 7A; see Methods).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach.

claim: When action selection is not fully determined by the striatum, efferent activity reflecting the selected action is critical for successful learning.
source: We found that when action selection is not fully determined by the striatum, such efferent activity is critical for successful learning (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented in Figure 7B.

claim: In the model, efferent activity has no effect on striatal action selection, due to the orthogonality of the sum and difference modes.
source: Notably, in our model, efferent activity has no effect on striatal action selection, due to the orthogonality of the sum and difference modes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a property of the model.

claim: In a hypothetical alternative model in which the iSPN plasticity rule is the same as that of dSPNs, the efferent activity needed for learning is not orthogonal to the output of the striatum, impairing off-policy learning.
source: In a hypothetical alternative model in which the iSPN plasticity rule is the same as that of dSPNs, the efferent activity needed for learning is not orthogonal to the output of the striatum, impairing off-policy learning (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of an alternative model presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Efferent excitation of opponent dSPNs/iSPNs is necessary both to implement correct learning updates given dSPN and iSPN plasticity rules, and to enable off-policy reinforcement learning.
source: Thus, efferent excitation of opponent dSPNs/iSPNs is necessary both to implement correct learning updates given dSPN and iSPN plasticity rules, and to enable off-policy reinforcement learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the theoretical and simulation results.

claim: Off-policy learning makes specific predictions about the dynamics of dopamine release.
source: We next asked whether other properties of striatal dynamics are consistent with off-policy reinforcement learning. We focused on the dynamics of dopamine release, as off-policy learning makes specific predictions about this signal.
evidence: This introduces the analysis of dopamine dynamics.

claim: Dopaminergic responses can be used as the learning signal for updating action selection in dorsal striatum in an 'actor-critic' architecture.
source: These dopaminergic responses can be used as the learning signal for a updating action selection in dorsal striatum (Equations 1 and 2), an arrangement commonly referred to as an 'actor-critic' architecture (Niv, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: When the striatal contribution to decision-making is weak, it is unable to learn the appropriate response when dopamine activity is modeled as a TD error.
source: The significance of on- versus off-policy learning algorithms can be demonstrated in simulations of operant conditioning tasks in which control of action selection is shared between the striatum and another 'tutor' pathway that biases responses toward the correct action. When the striatal contribution to decision-making is weak, it is unable to learn the appropriate response when dopamine activity is modeled as a TD error (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented in Figure 7D.

claim: A Q-learning model of dopamine activity enables efficient striatal learning even when control is shared with another pathway.
source: On the other hand, a Q-learning model of dopamine activity enables efficient striatal learning even when control is shared with another pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented in Figure 7D.

claim: The Q-learning model matches the dopamine data significantly better than alternatives.
source: The Q-learning model matches the data significantly better than alternatives (Figure 7E), providing support for a model of dorsal striatum as an off-policy reinforcement learning system.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 7E.

claim: The Q-learning model provides support for a model of dorsal striatum as an off-policy reinforcement learning system.
source: The Q-learning model matches the data significantly better than alternatives (Figure 7E), providing support for a model of dorsal striatum as an off-policy reinforcement learning system.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of experimental data.
